por-b-santa-luzia.s: The town of Viana do Castelo stands where the River Lima flows into the ocean. Above it rises the Santa Luzia hill. At the top there is a white church with a big dome, and you can go up by funicular. From the top you can see everything at once: the town’s roofs, the winding river, the blue ocean and the faraway mountains. On a clear day, it is a joy for the eyes. And then you don’t want to go back down at all.
a: The town, the river and the ocean

por-b-gil-eannes.s: In the port of Viana do Castelo stands an old ship called Gil Eannes. In the past it sailed after the fishing boats, far out into the cold sea. The fishermen lived far from home for a long time, and if anyone fell ill, the ship came to help, like a floating hospital. Now it no longer sails, and has become a museum: you can walk along the deck, peek into the cabins and see how the sailors lived.

por-b-ponte-de-lima.s: In the town of Ponte de Lima, a long stone bridge crosses the river. Part of it was built by the Romans, and then, in the Middle Ages, new arches were added. That is why the arches are different: some are older, some younger. People walk across the bridge, and flower gardens grow all around. The name of the town means just that: “the bridge over the Lima”. It is one of the oldest towns in Portugal.
a: The bridge over the River Lima

por-b-geres-park.s: Portugal has many nature parks, but only one national park: Peneda-Gerês. It is in the north, by the border with Spain, and it was created in nineteen seventy-one. It has mountains, forests, rivers and waterfalls, and also old villages made of stone. Wolves, roe deer, eagles and wild horses live in the park. People come here to walk, to swim and to listen to the quiet.

por-b-granaries.s: In the village of Soajo, in the Peneda-Gerês park, there are stone barns called espigueiros. They are long and narrow, and each one stands on thick stone legs. This is done on purpose. The wind blows underneath and dries the grain and the corn, and mice cannot climb up. On top of the barns there are often little crosses. From far away they look like a row of tiny stone houses.
a: So the wind dries the grain and mice cannot climb up
So the snow does not flood them

por-b-geres-springs.s: In the village of Gerês, warm water bubbles up out of the ground. They say the Romans already knew the hot springs in these mountains. They came here to bathe and to get well. Now there are modern baths nearby. The water is warm, clear and has no smell. All around, the mountains are covered with green forests, and the air is clean and fresh, so it is extra nice to get warm here.

por-b-roman-milestones.s: A Roman road runs through the Gerês mountains. Two thousand years ago, travellers, soldiers and traders walked along it. Beside the road stood little stone posts with writing that showed the distance to the town. Many of them are still standing, covered in moss. You walk along a forest path and suddenly you see one. It is like a letter from deep in the past.

por-b-fisgas-waterfall.s: In the Alvão mountains, in the north of Portugal, there is a waterfall called Fisgas do Ermelo. People call it one of the biggest waterfalls in the country. The water tumbles down the rocks in several steps, and the whole height is, they say, about two hundred metres. Tiny drops of spray hang in the air, and sometimes a rainbow stands over them. A path runs beside it, so you can walk up to the water. Down below it is so loud that you have to speak up.

por-b-cows.s: In the mountains of the north, cows of old local breeds graze. Barrosã cows have long horns, curved like a lyre or a harp. Cachena cows are quite small and dark reddish-brown, with lovely horns. In summer they are often taken to graze on high mountain meadows, and in winter they come back to the village. The local people are proud of these cows and take good care of their breed.

por-b-miranda-donkey.s: In the north-east of Portugal live Miranda donkeys. They are big, with thick fur and large ears. They are calm and kind. Long ago they carried people and loads along narrow paths. Now there are only a few left, and people take care of them. On a farm you can stroke the donkeys and feed them carrots. In winter their thick fur keeps them from the cold.

por-b-foz-coa.s: By the River Côa, not far from where it flows into the Douro, pictures were found on the rocks. They were scratched there by people who lived here a very long time ago. The oldest pictures are, they say, about thirty thousand years old. The ancient artists drew horses, deer, bulls and wild goats with thin lines right on the stone. Today the place is called Foz Côa. A park for visitors was made there, and UNESCO protects the pictures.

por-b-miranda-language.s: In Portugal people speak Portuguese. But near the town of Miranda do Douro, by the border with Spain, people also speak Mirandese. It is very old, and you can hear a bit of Portuguese and a bit of Spanish in it. Mirandese became an official language in nineteen ninety-nine. Now it is taught in schools, so that it does not disappear.
a: Near the town of Miranda do Douro

por-b-braganca-domus.s: In the town of Bragança, in the north-east of Portugal, there is an unusual old building called the Domus Municipalis. It was built of stone in the Middle Ages, and nobody knows the exact year for sure. Its walls are not square. They have five sides: there are five walls. They say the people of the town used to meet there to decide important things. Next to it stands a castle with a tall tower. Buildings like this are very rare.

por-b-douro-train.s: An old train runs along the River Douro and winds and wiggles with it all the way. The rails are laid almost right by the water. Out of the window you see vineyards on the slopes, then quiet water, then a stone bridge. The train goes slowly, as if it were enjoying the views itself. If you ride in the carriage, you can sit by the window and count the boats on the river.

por-b-almond-blossom.s: At the end of winter, in the north-east of Portugal, in the land of Trás-os-Montes, the almond trees come into flower. Their branches fill with white and pink blossoms while it is still cold all around. From far away it looks as if light snow is lying on the ground. People come to walk among the flowers. And later the almonds ripen on the trees.

por-c-sanzhuan-molotki.s: On the night of the twenty-fourth of June, Porto celebrates São João, the day of Saint John. The streets are full of people, and almost everyone holds a toy plastic hammer that squeaks in a funny way. People tap each other gently on the head with it for fun, then laugh and walk on. Long ago, they say, bunches of leeks were used instead of hammers. This joke is thought to bring good luck.

por-c-sanzhuan-manzheriku.s: For São João in Porto, people give each other little pots of sweet-smelling basil called manjerico. A paper flower is stuck in the soil, and a little note with a four-line poem is pinned to it. The poem says something kind or funny, often about love. The pot is put on the windowsill, and the whole room smells of summer. You can sniff the leaves, but this kind of basil is not eaten.
a: A note with a four-line poem

por-c-sanzhuan-sardiny.s: On São João night, the streets of Porto smell of smoke. Right by the houses, sardines are grilled on little barbecues. The fish is not put on a plate. It goes on a thick slice of bread, which soaks up the juice and becomes tasty too. People eat with their hands, sitting at long tables with their neighbours. Portuguese people love sardines so much that in June almost everyone eats them.

por-c-sanzhuan-ogni.s: At night on São João, festive fireworks burst over the River Douro. Thousands of people gather to watch. Some stand on the riverside, some on the high bridge, some on the hill above the city. The lights shine in the dark water, and it seems the fireworks are both in the sky and below it. That night children stay up later than usual, and in the morning the city quietly sleeps in.

por-c-barselush-petuh.s: An old legend tells of the town of Barcelos. A traveller was wrongly accused, and the judge was just about to give a harsh sentence. The traveller pointed at a roasted rooster on the table and said, “If I am right, it will crow.” And the rooster stood up on the dish and crowed! The judge believed him and let the traveller go. Since then the rooster of Barcelos has become a sign of good luck, and later of all Portugal.
a: Stood up on the dish and crowed

por-c-barselush-yarmarka.s: In Barcelos, a market is held every Thursday on the big square. People sell clay roosters, dishes, lace, baskets, cheeses, bread and fresh vegetables. The sellers call out loudly, and the buyers bargain and taste treats. Many people come from nearby villages just for this day. People often take a painted rooster home from Barcelos, for good luck.

por-c-barselush-rosa-ramalyu.s: Near Barcelos lived a potter called Rosa Ramalho. She made out of clay not only jugs but also figures: people, animals and made-up creatures with horns. Her figures came out funny and a little mysterious. When Rosa was no longer young, artists heard about her, and then the whole country. Today her work is shown in museums, and her grandchildren and great-grandchildren are learning to work the same way.

por-c-viana-serdtse.s: In the city of Viana do Castelo, they make famous golden hearts. The craftsman pulls out very thin gold wire, weaves a pattern from it and bends it into the shape of a heart with curls. The jewel comes out light as lace, but it is made of metal. These hearts are worn on the neck, and in the north of Portugal they are a sign of love. They are often passed down from mother to daughter.

por-c-syr-za-gorami.s: In the north-east of Portugal there is a land called Trás-os-Montes. Its name means “beyond the mountains”: the places there are far away and high. Shepherds graze sheep and make a cheese called terrincho from their milk. Young cheese is soft and creamy, and when it has aged, the taste becomes stronger. All around it is quiet, and on the meadows you can hear little bells. They say that in such a faraway place the cheese is especially tasty.

por-c-hleb-broa.s: In the north of Portugal, people bake a bread called broa. It is kneaded from corn flour and rye flour, so it is dark and dense. Its crust is thick and crunchy, and the inside is a little sweet. The broa from Avintes, near Porto, is especially famous. People eat it with soup, with cheese and with sardines. This bread smells of fields and a warm oven.

por-c-pao-de-lo-ovar.s: In the town of Ovar they bake a special sponge cake called pão de ló. It has lots of eggs in it, especially yolks, and that is why it is yellow like the sun. It is not baked all the way through, so the middle stays soft, almost like thick cream. The crust on top is thin, and inside it all runs onto the spoon. This cake is often baked for celebrations, and in a big family it disappears in minutes.

por-c-aveyru-yaichnye.s: In the city of Aveiro they make sweets called ovos moles. Inside there is a soft, sweet filling made of egg yolks and sugar, and outside there is a thin, crunchy wafer. The wafers are shaped like shells, little fish and tiny barrels, because the city stands by the water. These sweets were invented long ago, they say in monasteries, and now they are sold in pretty painted boxes.

por-c-aveyru-moliseyru.s: Long, narrow boats called moliceiros glide over the lagoon around Aveiro. They have a high, curved bow, and on their sides there are funny pictures and words, sometimes even jokes. Long ago, such boats were used to collect seaweed to feed the fields. Now they take tourists for rides, and you can float slowly while herons and gulls glide around. The boats look like dressed-up gondolas.

por-c-eyro-dom.s: In the villages of Soajo and Lindoso in the north of Portugal there are stone barns on legs. They are called espigueiros. They are narrow and long, like little houses. People keep corn cobs in them, so they dry and do not rot. The whole barn is built of stone, and gaps are left in the walls. The wind blows through them, and the grains stay dry even in damp weather.
a: So the wind dries the corn
So you can see the street

por-c-eyro-kresty.s: If you walk between the espigueiro barns, you can see that many have a little stone cross on the roof. From above, a barn often looks like a tiny church. In Lindoso a whole village of them stands there. By some counts there are more than fifty little stone houses, shoulder to shoulder. The oldest of them, they say, are already several hundred years old.

por-c-eyro-myshi.s: The espigueiro barns stand on stone pillars, and on top of each pillar lies a flat, round stone, like a hat. A mouse climbs up the pillar, reaches the hat, and then it cannot go any further, because the stone sticks out. That is how the corn grains stay whole. This is how people invented protection from mice and rats without locks or traps, and it still works today.
a: Flat stone hats on the pillars

por-c-kukuruza-iz-za-okeana.s: Long ago, people in Europe did not know corn. It grew in America, and sailors brought it on their ships about five hundred years ago. In the rainy north-west of Portugal, corn took root better than many other grains. People began to bake bread from it and to cook thick porridge. Now yellow fields are as much a part of the north as vineyards and hills.

por-c-poveu-podpisi.s: In the fishing town of Póvoa de Varzim, every family had its own sign made of straight lines and angles, like a mysterious rune. The sign passed from father to son. It was carved or painted on boats, on oars and on other things. That way you could tell at once whose thing it was. These signs are called “siglas poveiras”, and people still remember them.
a: Their own sign made of lines

por-c-svitery-povua.s: In Póvoa de Varzim, fishermen wore warm knitted woollen sweaters. On top of the knitting, patterns were embroidered in red, white or black thread. The wives, sisters and mums of the fishermen did the embroidery, and they hid loving messages in the patterns. Such a sweater is called a “camisola poveira”. These days such sweaters are not made so often, and each one looks like a little work of art.

por-c-vila-du-konde-korabli.s: In the town of Vila do Conde, by the River Ave, ships have been built since long ago. A big sailing ship by the riverside reminds us of this. It is a copy of an old Portuguese ship of the sixteenth century, and it was put by the museum about twenty years ago. You can climb aboard, walk along the deck and peek inside. At once you imagine how sailors set off on such a ship into the ocean.
a: A copy of an old sailing ship

por-c-poezd-vdol-doru.s: One of the most beautiful railways in Portugal runs from Porto along the River Douro. The rails run sometimes right by the water, sometimes above it, sometimes through tunnels. Outside the window you see terraces of grapes, boats and white houses. You should travel without hurry, and you can just watch the river valley float past. Many people go just for the sake of the journey.

por-c-poezd-pinyan.s: At Pinhão station, in the north of Portugal, the walls are covered with blue pictures made of tiles. They show vineyards, grape pickers and boats on the River Douro. While you wait for the train, you can look at a whole story. The pictures were made about ninety years ago, and they are still bright. The train comes, but you do not want to leave right away.

por-c-poezd-vuga.s: Not far from Aveiro, a little train runs on the Vouga line. The rails here are narrower than usual, so the carriages are narrow and small too. It rattles along slowly through valleys, past fields and streams, and stops in tiny villages. It feels as if the train is paying a visit to everyone. The narrow-gauge line still works today, and riding on it is a real adventure.

por-c-poezd-parovoz.s: In summer, an old train runs through the Douro valley. Its carriages are from the early twentieth century, with wooden benches, and an old locomotive pulls it. Sometimes, long ago, it was a real steam engine that puffed and let out steam. The train goes from Régua to Tua, without hurry, past the river, the vineyards and little stations. You sit by the window and feel as if you have gone back a hundred years.
a: Old ones, from the early twentieth century

por-c-karetush-podene.s: In the village of Podence, the caretos come out at carnival. They are people in bright costumes. The costume is sewn from long, coloured strips of wool, and a mask is put on the face. Bells jingle on the caretos’ belts. They run through the village, make a racket and playfully chase people. This carnival is on UNESCO’s list of intangible heritage.

por-c-lima-zabvenie.s: An old legend tells that when the ancient Romans came to the north of Portugal, they saw the River Lima. The soldiers decided it was the river of forgetting: whoever crossed it would forget everything. They were afraid to cross. Then the commander went into the water himself and crossed to the other bank. Then he called every soldier by name. Everyone understood that their memory was still there, and they followed him.

por-c-mirandesh-yazyk.s: You will be surprised, but in Portugal people do not only speak Portuguese. In the north-east, in the town of Miranda do Douro, there lives a language called Mirandese. It is like Portuguese but sounds different, and people speak it at home and at school. It became an official language in 1999. And in Miranda there is also a dance with sticks: dancers in skirts bang wooden sticks against each other in time with the music.

por-c-viana-kovry.s: In August, the festival of Senhora da Agonia is held in Viana do Castelo. The streets are decorated with carpets, but not made of thread: they are made of coloured sawdust, petals and salt. People make them at night, before the festival, and draw the patterns right on the road. In the morning the streets look like a many-coloured fairy tale. Then the procession walks over the carpets, but nobody is sad, because next year there will be new ones.

por-c-treska-bakalau.s: The best-loved fish in Portugal is bacalhau, which is dried, salted cod. It was caught far away in the cold northern seas, then salted and dried so it would not go bad on the way. Before cooking, it is soaked in water for a long time. They say there are so many bacalhau recipes that there is one for every day of the year. That is why the north and the south of the country each have their own favourite dishes with this fish.
a: Soak it in water for a long time

pt-n-estrela.s: Serra da Estrela means “the Star Mountains”. They are the highest mountains on the mainland of Portugal, if we don’t count the islands. In winter there is real snow, and children go sledging and skiing. A big, shaggy dog lives in these mountains too: the Estrela Mountain Dog. For many centuries it guarded sheep from wolves, but with its own family it is gentle and kind.

pt-n-pico.s: The highest mountain in Portugal stands in the middle of the ocean, in the Azores. It is the Pico volcano, more than two thousand three hundred metres high, and the island around it is called Pico too. On the very top there is another little hill, which people lovingly call Piquinho. In winter snow covers the peak, and the mountain looks like ice cream in a cone. Clouds often float below the top, like a white blanket.
a: On an island in the middle of the ocean
On the roof of a school

pt-n-furnas.s: On the island of São Miguel there is a valley called Furnas. The ground there is so hot that steam comes out of it and hot springs bubble. Cooks put meat, sausages, potatoes and cabbage into a big pot, put the lid on, and bury it in the hot ground by the lake. After about six hours they dig the pot up, and inside, lunch is ready: it is called cozido. The volcano cooked it itself!

pt-n-cha.s: Tea needs warmth and rain, so in Europe it hardly grows anywhere. But on the island of São Miguel in the Azores, tea has been grown for more than a hundred years. The tea bushes are trimmed in neat rows, and the green hills become stripy, like a jumper. In spring and summer, people pick the youngest little leaves and dry them, and that makes tea.

pt-n-cesto.s: On the island of Madeira, people go sledging with no snow at all! These sledges are woven wicker basket chairs on wooden runners. Two men in white clothes and straw hats push the sledge, run beside it and steer. And they brake with their own boots, which have thick rubber soles. That is how the sledge races down the streets for about two kilometres, from the village of Monte down towards Funchal. People have been riding like this for more than a hundred years.

pt-n-lince.s: The Iberian lynx is a wild cat with a spotted coat, tassels on its ears and fluffy whiskers on its cheeks. It lives only in Portugal and Spain, and what it likes to hunt most is rabbits. Once, very few of these lynxes were left, fewer than a hundred. People began to look after them, raise the babies and set them free. Now there are more than two thousand, and lynxes run over the hills of Portugal again.

pt-n-konki.s: In the south of Portugal, in the Algarve, there is a warm lagoon called Ria Formosa. Seahorses live there among the underwater grass. They swim standing up and hold on to the blades of grass with their tails, as if holding a rope. And the most amazing thing: the dad carries the babies! He keeps the eggs in a little pouch on his tummy, until tiny seahorses swim out of it. People take care of this lagoon, so that the seahorses have somewhere to live.

pt-n-batalha.s: In the town of Batalha stands a huge monastery, covered in stone patterns like lace. Almost six hundred years ago, the king ordered one more big hall with chapels to be added to it. The masters carved tall arches and fine patterns out of stone, but they never built the roof. That is why these chapels are called the Unfinished Chapels. Instead of a ceiling they have the sky: birds fly in, and rain drips right inside.

pt-n-tomar.s: In the town of Tomar, on a hill, stands a fortress built by the Knights Templar. Inside it hides an amazing round church: the Charola. It is more than eight hundred years old. Outside, it has sixteen walls, and it looks like a huge drum. Inside, everything is covered in paintings and shines with gold. There is an old legend that the knights rode in there on their horses.

pt-n-marvao.s: Marvão is a little village on top of a high rock. Strong stone walls surround it on every side, and a castle stands right at the edge. From far away the village looks like an eagle’s nest. You can see very far from here, even Spain next door. And when fog lies in the valleys below, it seems that the village is floating on the clouds.

pt-n-berlengas.s: Not far from the town of Peniche, right in the ocean, lie the Berlengas islands. On a tiny islet there stands an old stone fortress, and a narrow stone bridge leads to it. There are almost no people on the islands, but there are thousands of birds! Seagulls cry, build nests right on the rocks and look sternly at the visitors. And the water all around is so clear that you can see little fish.

pt-n-pao-por-deus.s: On the first of November, children in Portugal take little cloth bags and go from door to door. They knock at the neighbours’ doors and say: “Pão por Deus!” The neighbours put rolls, nuts, chestnuts, pomegranates and sweets into their bags. This custom is very old: even the great-grandmothers and great-grandfathers of today’s children did it. And the children often decorate their bags themselves.

pt-n-saudade.s: In the Portuguese language there is a special word: “saudade”. It is very hard to translate into other languages. Saudade is when you miss someone you love, or a place where you were happy. It is a little bit sad, but warm too, because you remember something good. When Grandma is far away and you remember her pies and her stories, that is saudade. The Portuguese sing fado songs about saudade.

pt-n-lingua.s: Portuguese is not spoken only in Portugal. You can hear it in Brazil in South America, in Angola and Mozambique in Africa, and even in East Timor in Asia. In all, more than two hundred million people speak it, and the most of them are in Brazil. See how far the language of a small country has travelled! And on the fifth of May, people celebrate World Portuguese Language Day.

pt-n-costa-nova.s: By the ocean, near the city of Aveiro, there is a village called Costa Nova. Its little houses are painted in wide stripes: red, blue, green, yellow, and always white too. It looks as if the houses have put on stripy pyjamas. Long ago there were wooden sheds here, where fishermen kept their nets. They say the bright stripes helped the fishermen to recognise their own house from far away, even in fog.

pt-n-a-cork-number.s: Cork oaks grow in Portugal. People take the bark off them, like peeling an orange, but the tree does not get ill from it. The new bark grows back, and it is taken off again only after about nine years. So that nobody forgets, the workers paint the last digit of the year on the trunk. If a tree has the number 5, it means it was undressed in a year that ends in five. Such an oak can live for about two hundred years and give people bark again and again.
a: To remember in which year the bark was taken off
So that birds do not sit on the branches

pt-n-a-cork-space.s: Do you know why cork does not sink in water? Inside it there are lots and lots of tiny air bubbles. Because of them, the bark of the cork oak is light, springy and lets heat through badly. The Portuguese make from it not only stoppers for bottles, but also soles, bags, hats and even floor tiles. And a thin layer of cork is put on rockets: it helps them not to get too hot when they fly through the air. That is how a piece of a Portuguese forest travels to the stars.
a: It has lots of tiny air bubbles inside
It is completely empty inside, like glass

pt-n-a-salt-castro.s: In the south of Portugal, near the little town of Castro Marim, the sea is let into shallow ponds. In summer the sun warms the water, it dries up into the air, and the salt is left behind. White heaps of salt lie right by the water and sparkle like snow. The most delicate salt is gathered from the top, from the surface of the water, with light wooden rakes. It is called “flor de sal”, “the salt flower”. You can crumble it with your fingers into thin, crunchy flakes.

pt-n-a-flamingo-sapal.s: Next to the salt ponds of the Algarve there are marshes where there are always lots of birds. Pink flamingos fly in here. They walk on their thin legs through shallow salty water and look for something with their beaks upside down. They catch tiny shrimps and algae, and this food turns their feathers pink. A baby flamingo is born grey and only becomes pink later. The birds are easy to see if you look from far away through binoculars.
a: Tiny shrimps and algae that they eat

pt-n-a-madeira-levada.s: On the island of Madeira the rain falls in the mountains, but the fields and gardens lie down below, where it is drier. Long ago people dug long, narrow ditches, so that water would run down by itself from the mountain to the fields. They are called “levadas”. Beside each one a level path was left, and today tourists walk along it. The levadas go through the forest, past waterfalls and along the edges of cliffs. You walk along the path, and beside you a stream babbles, and it shows you the way itself.
a: So that water from the mountains flows to the fields and gardens
So that boats can sail on them
To scare birds away from the vegetable garden

pt-n-a-madeira-fanal.s: On the island of Madeira a very old laurel forest has survived. It has been growing here for millions of years, and UNESCO protects it. One of the most fairytale places is the forest clearing of Fanal. Old, twisted trees stand there, covered in moss, and often mist floats between them. The forest seems magical, as if a forest giant might step out at any moment. The very word “Madeira” means “wood”: long ago the island was almost entirely covered in forest.

pt-n-a-desertas-seals.s: Not far from Madeira there are three uninhabited rocky islands, the Desertas. Very rare monk seals live there. They say they got this name because of their round head and the folds on their neck, which look like a monk’s hood. Once, very few of these animals were left, and the islands were made a nature reserve, so that nobody would disturb the seals. People look after them, and more and more baby seals are born. The seals warm themselves on the rocks and dive for fish.

pt-n-a-cabo-girao.s: On the island of Madeira there is one of the highest sea cliffs in Europe: Cabo Girão, about five hundred and eighty metres high. A viewing platform with a see-through glass floor has been built there. You step onto it and see, far below, tiny houses, little boats and vegetable plots on narrow terraces. It feels as if you are hanging in the air, like a bird. Down below, right by the water, people grow vegetables on small ledges, which a cable car goes down to.

pt-n-a-porto-santo-sand.s: Next to Madeira lies the little island of Porto Santo. Almost all the beaches on Madeira are made of pebbles, but here golden sand stretches for about nine kilometres. You can walk along the warm, shallow shore for a very long time and never reach the end. The water by the shore is calm and clear, so little children splash about there without fear. People say the sand on the island is good for your health, and many lie in it, buried up to their necks.
a: A long beach with golden sand
A beach of white shells where you cannot swim

pt-n-a-sete-cidades.s: On the island of São Miguel, in the Azores, lies a huge ancient bowl. In it stand two lakes side by side, joined by a narrow strip of water. One lake is blue and the other is green. People tell a legend, and in different versions it is a little different: a princess and a shepherd fell in love, but they were not allowed to meet. They cried, and their tears became the lakes: in one version the princess’s eyes were blue, and the shepherd’s eyes were green. The place is called Sete Cidades.

pt-n-a-azores-hydrangea.s: In the Azores, every summer, hydrangeas burst into bloom along the roads. They are bushes with huge caps of flowers: blue, lilac and pink. They were planted instead of fences, to protect the fields from the wind. Whole rows of flowers stretch along the slopes all the way to the ocean. The colour depends on the soil: in volcanic soil many flowers turn blue. That is why the Azores are sometimes called the “blue islands”.
a: Instead of fences, to protect from the wind
So that the cows would not get lost
So that ships could find the port

pt-n-a-azores-pineapple.s: Pineapples love hot countries, but in the Azores they are grown even though the weather is mild and cool. For this they are planted in warm glass greenhouses. A pineapple grows very slowly, for about two years, until it becomes sweet and juicy. The Azorean pineapple turns out small, but very fragrant. On the island of São Miguel you can see long rows of prickly plants under glass roofs, and even smell a ripe fruit yourself.
a: On top of a mountain, under snow

pt-n-a-azores-whales.s: All around the Azores the ocean is very deep, and whales and dolphins live in it. Tourists go out in boats and watch them from a distance. Most of all there are sperm whales, toothed whales with a huge square head. They dive to a great depth for squid and can stay under water for a long time. Above the water the sperm whale lifts its tail, and then it blows a little spout. Dolphins often swim next to the boat, as if saying hello.

pt-n-a-algar-carvao.s: On the island of Terceira there is a cave called Algar do Carvão. It looks like a giant well: long ago, lava rose through it from the volcano. Now the lava has long gone cold, and you can go down inside by steps, about ninety metres. From above, the sky shines through the hole, and ferns grow all around. Down below you can see stone icicles: they are icicles made of silica, not ice. Deep down lies a quiet little lake, and water gathers there in the cave.

pt-n-a-capelinhos-island.s: In 1957, near the island of Faial, smoke and ash rose out of the water in the ocean for many months. A volcano woke up under the water, and a new piece of land appeared next to the island. The island became bigger! The place was named Capelinhos. The new land is grey and empty, like on another planet, and there stands a lighthouse, half buried in ash. Today people come here to see how islands are born, and to walk on this land.
a: The island grew bigger, and new land appeared
The island sank under the water
A forest grew on the island in one night

pt-n-a-azores-flores.s: One of the farthest islands of the Azores is called Flores. In Portuguese “flores” means “flowers”. There is so much rain here that the island looks like a green garden. Dozens of waterfalls fall from steep cliffs, and between them lie lakes in round volcanic bowls. Hydrangeas bloom along the roads. The island is small, and there are few people on it. It is quiet here, and you can hear the water falling and the birds singing.

pt-n-a-almond-blossom.s: In the Algarve there is no snow in winter, but in January and February the almond trees bloom. The trees are covered in white and pink flowers, and it seems that the fields are strewn with snow. There is an old legend. A Moorish king took a princess from the north as his wife, and she missed the snow. So the king planted lots of almond trees on the hills, and when they bloomed, the princess smiled: everything around was white, just like at home.

pt-n-a-ponta-piedade.s: Not far from the town of Lagos in the Algarve, the sea has carved real castles out of golden rocks. For centuries the waves worked on the stone, and there are arches, little towers, narrow passages and small caves. This place is called Ponta da Piedade. Fishermen and tourists sail in little boats right between the stone walls, and under the bottom of the boat the water is clear and turquoise. The boat quietly enters a dim grotto where the echo repeats every word.
a: The sea, the waves over many years
The wind, which blew for one year

pt-n-a-chameleon.s: Not everyone knows that chameleons live in the Algarve. They sit on the branches of pine trees and bushes, and they are hard to spot. Their skin changes colour, and the little animal blends in with the leaves. A chameleon’s eyes move on their own: one looks forward, the other looks back. Its tongue is longer than its body, and it catches flies with it. The chameleon walks slowly, as if it is very afraid of falling off the branch.
a: With its tail, like a lasso

pt-n-a-alqueva-stars.s: In the south of Portugal, in the Alentejo, there is a big lake called Alqueva. Fields and hills lie around it, and there are few towns with bright lights. At night it is dark here, so you can see a great many stars. Above your head the pale stripe of the Milky Way stretches out, as if someone had spilled milk. This place is thought to be one of the best in Europe for watching the stars. People come here with telescopes and lie down on the grass just to look up.
a: There are few lights and the sky is dark
The stars are closer to the ground there
There is always a full moon there

pt-n-a-storks-cliffs.s: White storks in Portugal usually build their nests on roofs, chimneys and poles. But in the south-west, by the ocean, in the Alentejo, they have made their homes on sea cliffs. It is one of very few places in the world where storks live like this. The nest stands on a rocky top above the waves, and below the surf roars. Every year the birds come back to the same home and mend it with new branches. Over the years the nest becomes huge.
a: On the beach, in the sand

pt-n-a-acorn-pigs.s: In the Alentejo there are light woods of cork oaks and holm oaks. This is called a “montado”. Black Iberian pigs wander under the trees. In autumn the ground is covered with acorns, and the pigs eat them as they walk over the hills. There are so many acorns that there is enough for everyone. Sheep graze nearby, and birds sit on the branches of the oaks. The oaks give shade, shelter and treats, and all the animals in the wood live together happily.

pt-n-a-estrela-dog.s: In the Serra da Estrela mountains lives an old breed of dog. It is called the Serra da Estrela mountain dog. The dog is big, with thick, warm fur that keeps out the cold and the wind. It guards the flock of sheep: it walks beside the shepherd and does not let strangers near the sheep. Although the dog is huge, it is kind and gentle with people. Estrela is the highest mountain on the mainland: almost two thousand metres, and in winter there is snow.

pt-n-a-dino-tracks.s: At Cabo Espichel, not far from Lisbon, huge footprints are left by the cliffs. They are the footprints of dinosaurs that walked here more than a hundred million years ago. Back then the ground was soft like mud, and the giants’ feet left deep dents. Later the mud hardened, and the footprints turned to stone. Now you can see them on the rocky slope: long lines of round holes, each one wider than a plate. These footprints were made by plant-eating dinosaurs with long necks.

pt-n-a-mira-caves.s: Not far from the town of Mira de Aire there is the biggest cave in Portugal that visitors can enter. You go down some stairs, and halls greet you with stone icicles growing from the ceiling and the floor. Inside it is cool and damp, always the same, in winter and in summer. The lights make the walls pink and golden. There is an underground waterfall where water flows, and a little lake where the stone arches are reflected.

pt-n-b-coimbra-bats.s: In Coimbra there is one of the oldest universities in Europe, and in it is the golden Joanina Library. It has tall carved bookcases and very old books. They are guarded by unusual guards: little bats! At night they fly out and catch the insects that like to nibble paper. And so that no marks are left on the tables overnight, in the evening the staff cover them with leather sheets. The books stay safe, and the bats are well fed.

pt-n-b-queen-isabel-roses.s: Long, long ago, Queen Isabel lived in Coimbra. She was kind and loved to help the poor. They say that one day she was carrying bread in her apron to give to the hungry. The king came towards her and asked, “What have you got there?” The queen answered, “Roses.” She opened her apron, and instead of bread there were fresh roses! This is only a beautiful legend, but in Portugal people still tell it today.

pt-n-b-coimbra-ribbons.s: In Coimbra students wear black capes and suits, and they also have a lovely tradition. In spring the city holds the Festival of the Ribbons. Each faculty has its own coloured ribbon, and the students proudly wear it on their bags. The streets are full of music, songs and parades. The name of the festival means “burning of the ribbons”: when school is over, the ribbons are burned in memory, as the tradition says.

pt-n-b-evora-diana-temple.s: The city of Évora is older than many people think: the Romans lived here long ago. They left a temple that has stood for almost two thousand years! The tall columns are still there, and heavy stone beams lie on top. People call it the Temple of Diana, but scientists are not sure it was really hers. But one thing is certain: the Romans built it, and it stands right in the middle of the city.

pt-n-b-cork-oak-years.s: Near Évora there are cork oaks, and people take bark from them. The bark is carefully cut off with a small axe, and the tree stays alive. Then the bark grows back! The next time it is taken off is about nine years later. So that nobody gets mixed up, the last number of the year is painted on the trunk. This bark is made into corks for bottles, bags and even soles for shoes.

pt-n-b-tomar-tabuleiros.s: In the town of Tomar, once every four years, there is the Festival of the Trays, the Tabuleiros. Girls in white walk through the streets, and on each girl’s head is a tall tower of loaves, as tall as the girl herself! The tower is decorated with ears of wheat and paper flowers, and a white dove sits on top. A helper walks beside her and holds it steady. After the parade the bread is given to those who need it.

pt-n-b-tomar-window.s: In Tomar, in a big monastery, there is a window that looks like a sea fairy tale. It is carved from stone, but on it there are thick ropes, sea knots, shells, seaweed and anchors. The masters made it at the time when the Portuguese sailed across the oceans and were very proud of their ships. This style is called Manueline. You look at the window and it is as if you can hear the sound of the waves.

pt-n-b-nazare-biggest-wave.s: In the town of Nazaré the ocean puts on a real wonder. Close to the shore a deep underwater canyon begins, and the waves in front of the beach grow to enormous sizes. In winter brave surfers come here. In 2020 the German Sebastian Steudtner rode a wave 26 metres and 21 centimetres high, taller than an eight-storey house! The record was written in the Guinness Book of Records.

pt-n-b-nazare-seven-skirts.s: Nazaré is an old fishing village, and the women here wear a special costume. They say the fisherwomen put on seven skirts, one on top of another! The skirts were bright and warm. While their husbands were out at sea, the women sat on the sand, mended nets and dried fish, and the skirts, they say, kept them warm in the wind. The number seven is explained in different ways: seven days of the week, seven colours of the rainbow. You can still see this costume at festivals.

pt-n-b-sagres-wind-rose.s: On the cape near Sagres lies a huge stone wheel about forty-three metres across. Stone lines spread out from the centre like rays. It is a wind rose, like a giant compass. Scientists still argue about what it was for: maybe to study the winds and the points of the compass. It can be seen best from above, and in the wind it is easy to imagine you are a sailor.

pt-n-b-eusebio-panther.s: Eusébio was born in Mozambique, in Africa, and then came to play in Portugal. He ran so fast and kicked the ball so hard that people called him the “Black Panther”. At the 1966 World Cup he scored nine goals and was the top scorer of the tournament. The Portugal team won the bronze medals then. Everyone loved Eusébio, both for his play and for his kind smile.

pt-n-b-ronaldo-madeira.s: Cristiano Ronaldo was born on the island of Madeira, in the city of Funchal. As a boy he played football in the street, and then he became one of the most famous footballers in the world. He has scored more goals for national teams than anyone in history. And today Funchal’s airport carries his name, and a bronze bust stands there. You land on the island and at once you see what the people are proud of.

pt-n-b-cabral-brazil.s: In 1500 Captain Cabral led a fleet towards India, but the ships were carried far to the west. The sailors saw a tall mountain and called it Easter Mountain, because it was Easter time. That is how they discovered Brazil! The scribe Caminha wrote the king a long letter. In it he told of green forests, bright parrots and people who welcomed the visitors with curiosity.

pt-n-b-dias-cape-storms.s: The Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias, in 1488, was the first European to sail round the very south of Africa. Strong winds blew there and the waves rocked the ship, and he called the place the Cape of Storms. But the king decided the name should be changed, because beyond this cape the way to India began. He called it the Cape of Good Hope. The cape still has this name today.

pt-n-b-gil-eanes-bojador.s: Long ago sailors were afraid of Cape Bojador, off the coast of Africa. People said that beyond it the sea boiled and ships never came back. But in 1434 the Portuguese sailor Gil Eanes sailed on all the same. He went round the cape and saw an ordinary sea and a sandy shore. He came back and told everyone: there is nothing to be afraid of! After that, sailors began to sail farther.
a: An ordinary sea and a shore

pt-n-b-caravel-ship.s: The Portuguese invented and improved a light ship, the caravel. It is small, quick and easy to steer, and it has triangular sails on its masts. Such sails let it go almost against the wind, in zigzags. Thanks to caravels, sailors could sail along unknown shores and come home again. Caravels were small: only about fifteen to twenty metres long.

pt-n-b-cante-alentejano.s: In the Alentejo region people sing a special song, the cante alentejano. Many people sing at once: men and women stand side by side, and one starts, and the others join in. You hear only voices, no guitar and no drum! In the past people sang like this in the fields, so that the work went more cheerfully. This song is very old, and in 2014 it was put on the UNESCO world heritage list.
a: People sing only to a drum

pt-n-b-portuguese-guitar.s: The Portuguese guitar has a round body that looks like a pear. And it has not six strings but twelve: they are grouped in six pairs. The sound is bright and silvery, like drops of rain. On the side of the guitar there are little tuning screws in the shape of a small fan. It is played in Portugal when people sing sad and beautiful songs.

pt-n-b-salvador-eurovision.s: Portugal has taken part in the Eurovision Song Contest since 1964. For more than fifty years the country waited for a win! And then in 2017 a young singer, Salvador Sobral, sang a quiet, gentle song, “Amar pelos dois”, which means “To Love for Both”. He sang in Portuguese, with no loud effects and no dancing. People in many countries voted for him, and Portugal won for the first time.

pt-n-b-bacalhau-cod.s: In Portugal people love dried and salted cod, called bacalhau. The fish was caught in the cold northern seas, then salted and dried so that it would not go bad for a long time. Then at home it had to be soaked in water. The Portuguese joke that they have a bacalhau recipe for every day of the year, or even more. It is boiled, baked and fried with potatoes.

pt-n-b-serra-estrela-cheese.s: In the Serra da Estrela mountains shepherds make a special sheep’s cheese. To make the milk thicken, they put in a prickly flower, the thistle. The cheese turns out soft and creamy. When it is cut open, it flows like thick cream. So the cheese is not cut into slices: you cut off the top and eat it with a spoon, spreading it on bread. It tastes gentle and a little spicy.

pt-n-b-bolo-rei.s: At Christmas in Portugal people bake a cake shaped like a big ring, the bolo-rei. It looks like a crown: on top lie pieces of dried fruit and nuts, like jewels. By tradition a bean is hidden inside. Whoever finds the bean in their slice buys the cake for the whole family the next year. So everyone at the table looks for it very carefully.

pt-n-b-magusto-chestnuts.s: In November Portugal celebrates St Martin’s Day. They say that at this time there are often warm sunny days, called “St Martin’s summer”. People gather round a bonfire for the festival called magusto. They roast chestnuts, which crackle and smell of smoke, and people eat them hot, straight away. The shells are thrown into a shared basket, and the children race to see who can peel them fastest.

pt-n-b-words-pan-marmalade.s: Portuguese sailors brought back not only goods but words. About five hundred years ago they sailed to Japan. Bread was new to the Japanese, and they began to call it “pan”, from the Portuguese word “pão”. And so it stayed! The word “marmalade” also came from Portuguese, where it meant jam made from quince. Quince in Portuguese is “marmelo”.

pt-n-b-aveiro-ovos-moles.s: In the town of Aveiro they invented a sweet called ovos moles. Inside there is a soft, sweet cream made of egg yolks and sugar. Outside there is a thin, crunchy shell made of wafer paste. The shells are made in the shape of seashells, little fish and tiny barrels. So you can see in the sweets that the town stands by the sea. The recipe has been kept for many years, and it is the town’s local pride.

ru-big.s: Russia is the biggest country in the world. You could fit more than one hundred and eighty countries the size of Portugal inside it! Russia is so wide that it has eleven time zones. When children in Kaliningrad go to bed, it is already morning in Kamchatka. The children there are waking up and getting ready for nursery.

ru-transsib.s: The longest railway in the world runs through Russia. It is called the Trans-Siberian Railway. A train takes almost a week to go from Moscow to Vladivostok! Outside the window you see forests, rivers, mountains and even Lake Baikal. On the train you can sleep on a bunk, drink tea and watch the country change. In Vladivostok, right by the sea, there is a post with the number 9288. That is how many kilometres the train has travelled.

ru-baikal.s: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world. Its water is so clean that you can see pebbles on the bottom, even very far down. In winter Baikal freezes, and the ice can be clear as glass. You look down at your feet and see water! Baikal is also home to the nerpa, a round seal with big dark eyes. You cannot find these seals anywhere else in the world, only in Lake Baikal.
a: An elephant in a stripy jumper

ru-geysers.s: Kamchatka is a land of volcanoes. It has many fire-breathing mountains, and some of them sometimes wake up and puff out smoke and ash. Kamchatka also has the Valley of Geysers. A geyser is a hot spring. Suddenly a fountain of boiling water and steam shoots out of it: pshhh! There are no roads to the valley, so visitors are flown there by helicopter.

ru-tiger.s: In the taiga, a thick forest in the Russian Far East, lives the Amur tiger. It is one of the biggest cats in the world. It is not afraid of snow or frost, because it has thick warm fur and a layer of fat under its skin. Every tiger has its own stripes, just like your fingerprints. That is how scientists tell tigers apart in pictures taken by cameras hidden in the forest.

ru-oymyakon.s: Oymyakon is a village in Yakutia. It is one of the coldest places on Earth where people live. In winter it can be colder than sixty degrees below zero! If you throw a cup of boiling water into the air there, it turns into a little cloud of snow at once. Yakut horses live outdoors all year. Their fur is thick and long, as warm as a fur coat. And in summer it can even get hot in Oymyakon.

ru-matryoshka.s: A matryoshka is a wooden doll with other dolls hiding inside it, each one smaller than the last. The first matryoshka was made more than a hundred years ago. It had eight dolls. The biggest was a girl holding a black rooster, and the smallest was a little baby in a blanket. This matryoshka is still kept today in a toy museum in the town of Sergiev Posad. People there still carve and paint matryoshkas.

ru-c-pelmeni.s: The word “pelmeni” comes from the Ural mountains. The Komi-Permyak people lived there, and in their language “pelnyan” means “bread ear”. Look at a pelmen: it really does look a bit like a tiny ear made of dough! In Siberia people made hundreds of them at once and put them out in the frost. The frozen pelmeni went into a sack, and a hunter took it along on his journey. Boil some water, and dinner is ready.

ru-maslenitsa.s: Maslenitsa is a merry festival to say goodbye to winter and welcome spring. For a whole week people make blini, which are thin pancakes: round, golden and hot like a little sun. They are eaten with sour cream, honey or jam. People slide down hills, dance in circles and have snowball fights. On the last day they burn a big straw doll called Maslenitsa. That is how they say goodbye to winter.

ru-d-belka-strelka.s: On 19 August 1960 two dogs, Belka and Strelka, flew into space. They travelled in a spaceship, went around the Earth 17 times and landed safely a day later. The dogs were cheerful, and people welcomed them home like heroes. Later Strelka had puppies, and one of them, called Pushinka, was given to the daughter of the American president, Caroline. People still remember Belka and Strelka today. There is even a cartoon about them.

ru-bears.s: Many big brown bears live in Kamchatka. In summer, lots of salmon swim from the sea up the rivers. The fish swim against the current and even jump over rocks and little waterfalls. The bears stand right in the river and catch them with their paws and teeth. That way they get nice and fat, so they can sleep all winter in their den.
a: To put them in a cupboard

ru-volga.s: The Volga is the longest river in Europe. It starts as a tiny stream that you can step over. Then it grows so wide that you can hardly see the other bank. Big boats sail on the Volga, and large cities stand along its banks. At the end of its long journey, the Volga flows into the Caspian Sea. People lovingly call it “Mother Volga”.

ru-elbrus.s: In the Caucasus mountains stands Elbrus, the highest mountain in Russia and in all of Europe. It is 5,642 metres tall! Elbrus has two white peaks, like the two humps of a camel. It is a sleeping volcano covered with snow and ice. Even in summer there is snow, and brave climbers go up in warm jackets and dark glasses.

ru-ustyug.s: Father Frost lives in the old town of Veliky Ustyug. His wooden house stands in the forest, not far from the town. Children from all over Russia send letters here, whole sacks of letters! Father Frost even has his own post office. He celebrates his birthday on the eighteenth of November. People say that is when the real frosts begin in Veliky Ustyug.
a: On the first of July, when it is hot

ru-kizhi.s: On Kizhi island, in the middle of Lake Onega, stands an amazing wooden church. It has twenty-two domes, round tops that look like little onions. It was built in 1714 almost without nails. The logs fit tightly together, like the pieces of a wooden building set. And the little wooden tiles on the domes shine in the sun like silver.

ru-murmansk.s: Murmansk is the biggest city north of the Arctic Circle, far in the north. In winter the polar night comes: for more than a month the sun does not show up in the sky at all. But sometimes the northern lights appear, green ribbons of light that wave like curtains in the wind. In summer it is the other way round: the sun shines all day and night and never goes to bed.
a: The sun shines even at night

ru-a-metro-dvortsy.s: The Moscow metro is not just trains. Many stations look like palaces, with marble, chandeliers and pictures made of tiny pieces of coloured glass on the ceiling. At the station called Revolution Square there are bronze statues of people. Next to them sits a bronze dog called Ingus. Passengers stroke her nose for luck, so the nose shines like gold. You can ride to get somewhere, or just ride around and look at the stations, like in a museum under the ground.
a: Her nose, which people stroke for luck

ru-b-kalan-kurily.s: The Kuril Islands are a long chain of about fifty islands between Kamchatka and Japan. In the cold waves near the shore lives the sea otter. It sleeps on its back in the water and wraps itself in seaweed so it does not drift away. The sea otter picks up shellfish from the seabed and cracks them open with a stone that it keeps in a fold of skin. Its fur is so thick that the water never reaches its body.
